text:
What an admirable day! The vast park swoons beneath the Sun’s burning gaze, as youth does beneath the dominion of Love.

The universal ecstasy of things is expressed by no sound; the very waters seem asleep. So unlike human festivities, this is a silent orgy.

One might say that an ever-increasing light gives things an ever-brighter glitter; that the excited flowers burn with desire to rival the blue of the sky through the force of their colors; and that the heat, making perfumes visible, lifts them toward the star like smoke.

But amid the universal joy I have seen one afflicted being.

At the feet of a colossal Venus, one of those artificial fools, one of those voluntary jesters charged with making kings laugh when remorse or weariness obsesses them, decked out in a brilliant and ridiculous costume, wearing horns and bells, crouches beside the pedestal and raises tear-filled eyes toward the immortal goddess.

And his eyes say: “I am the last and loneliest of human beings, deprived of love and friendship; I am far below the most imperfect animal. Yet I too was made to understand and feel immortal beauty. Alas, Goddess! Have pity on my sadness and my delirium!”

But the implacable Venus gazes far away at I know not what with her marble eyes.

translation.title: The Fool and the Venus
translation.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The prose paragraphs and the contrast between universal ecstasy and the fool’s exclusion are preserved.
